title: Progressive flush probe labbook
body:
Summary:

This labbook records an exploration of "progressive flush" patterns from clients into the serving chain and how various proxy pacing behaviors and HTTP/gRPC framing interact with KV cache warmup and tail latency. The goal was not to ship a feature but to surface micro-behaviors that cause p95/p99 regressions in real workloads that use streaming generation (token-by-token, client flushes) and to document mitigations.

Background and motivation:
- We frequently see customer apps using a mix of small-client-side flushes (websocket-like apps, server SDKs that flush every token or punctuation) and larger batched requests (server-side batching).
- When those small flushes traverse a proxy (Envoy in our testbed) or an ingress edge that implements pacing/queueing, we observe unexpected amplification of tail latency and spiky CPU due to chatty socket writes and HTTP2 flow-control interactions.
- Hypothesis: a combination of small flush sizes + moderate client flush interval leads to inefficient kernel/TCP behaviors, poor coalescing in proxy, increased head-of-line blocking on HTTP2 streams, and suboptimal batching decisions in the serving runtime.

Experiment goals:
1) Measure how incremental flush intervals (0ms, 8ms, 25ms, 50ms, 100ms) and flush sizes (1 token ~ 64B, 8 tokens ~ 512B, 32 tokens ~ 2KB) affect latency percentiles and throughput across three network/proxy stacks (direct, Envoy http2, Envoy http1.1 chunked).
2) Observe proxy queue behavior (per-stream queue length, buffer occupancy) and how proxy pacing windowing influences bursts reaching the runtime.
3) Evaluate mitigations: client-side coalescing heuristics, aggressive Nagle toggling (TCP_NODELAY on/off), and proxy-level frame coalescing (Envoy filter prototype).

Testbed and setup:
- Client harness: in-house harness (stream-probe) that can emit streaming requests with configurable flush interval and flush-size. 200 concurrent simulated users, Poisson arrival of new streams, each stream requests a 64-token generation.
- Serving runtime: lightweight inference simulator that returns tokens at deterministic 6ms/token to emulate transformer decoder work and allows toggling of KV cache warmup penalties.
- Proxies: (A) none (direct connection), (B) Envoy with HTTP/2 multiplexing default settings, (C) Envoy with HTTP/1.1 chunked transfer (client->proxy->runtime uses chunked POSTs).
- Network conditions: baseline lab network ~10ms RTT, limited to 200Mbps per node. Additional experiments included 30ms RTT and 1% packet loss to simulate mobile-ish conditions.
- Metrics collected: p50/p95/p99 end-to-end response time (first token, full stream completion), tokens/sec, CPU load on proxy and runtime nodes, kernel socket queues (TX/RX queue lengths), Envoy per-stream buffer sizes, and serving runtime batch sizes and batch latency.

Key findings:
1) Flush interval dominates p99 under multiplexed HTTP/2: when clients flush every token (0ms or <=8ms), p99 increases 2.5x compared to coalesced flushes (25ms+). The reason appears to be increased HTTP2 frame fragmentation and interleaving that causes head-of-line delays in Envoy when multiple small frames compete.
2) HTTP/1.1 chunked performed slightly better for tiny flushes vs HTTP/2 in our Envoy config, because chunked bodies produced fewer multiplexed frames and allowed connection-level coalescing at the kernel layer. However, HTTP/1.1 lost the benefits of stream multiplexing when parallelism increased, leading to connection saturation earlier.
3) Proxy pacing/windowing (Envoy default) introduced measurable batching of writes to downstream; with small flush sizes this created micro-bursts: many tiny writes queued then flushed together, spiking CPU and causing transient queueing at the runtime ingress. This amplified inference queuing and increased effective end-to-end p99.
4) Disabling TCP_NODELAY on the client side (i.e., letting Nagle coalesce) reduced syscalls and improved p95/p99 for flush intervals between 8ms and 50ms, but increased first-token latency for very low concurrency workloads. There is a tradeoff: coalescing reduces CPU/syscall overhead, but adds latency when the client expects immediate delivery.
5) KV cache warmup sensitivity: streams that emit many small flushes keep the KV cache warmer per-stream (since tokens arrive and are appended gradually), but because proxy micro-bursts delay when the runtime receives the tokens, batching decisions sometimes grouped unrelated concurrent streams and wasted batch slots, reducing tokens/sec efficiency.

Mitigations tested and results:
- Client-side coalescing heuristic (flush if either N tokens buffered or X ms elapsed, with X=25ms and N=8): this gave the best overall balance across all proxy modes — p99 improved by ~40% versus uncoalesced tiny-flush baseline and tokens/sec remained within 10% of optimal.
- Adaptive Nagle strategy: set TCP_NODELAY dynamically based on concurrency and observed RTT. Works well in controlled SDK environments but is brittle for generic browser clients.
- Envoy per-connection write coalescer (experimental filter): by coalescing small frames into larger frames and respecting stream priorities we reduced CPU spikes and lowered p99 by ~18% vs baseline Envoy. Implementation complexity high and needs careful tuning for priority inversion cases.
- Runtime admission tweak: prefer to batch by arrival time window rather than strict head-of-queue up to a small extra delay (e.g., 5-10ms). This reduced wasted batch slots caused by bursts of delayed tiny writes and improved overall tokens/sec ~7%.

Observations and non-obvious behaviors:
- When mixing HTTP/2 multiplexing with long-lived streams (many small writes), priority and flow-control interplay in Envoy can starve newer parallel streams — even though connection-level throughput is adequate, older busy streams hold flow-control windows.
- Kernel-level coalescing was surprisingly important. On Linux 5.x, sendmmsg/sendfile patterns that reduce syscalls helped proxy CPU but required careful handling of HTTP/2 frames to avoid violating framing semantics.
- Under simulated packet loss (1%), small flush sizes produced many retransmits; the overhead magnified latency variance and made coalescing even more beneficial.

Recommended short-term actions (owner + rough ETA):
- SDK: ship experimental client coalescing option in JS/Python SDKs (owner: Mason Li, ETA: 3 weeks). Default off for compatibility, opt-in via config flag.
- Envoy: prototype a coalescing write filter that groups small stream frames up to configurable window (owner: Diego Alvarez, ETA: 6 weeks for prototype). Add data-plane tests for priority interactions.
- Runtime: implement arrival-window batching knob (5-15ms) and canary to measure quality impact (owner: eng-serving-runtime infra team, ETA: 2 weeks).
- Docs: add guidance in "Streaming performance" section of public docs recommending client flush heuristics and noting tradeoffs for HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 (owner: Aisha Patel, ETA: 1 week).

Open questions / next experiments:
- Browser clients and HTTP semantics: how to provide safe default coalescing that respects streaming UX? (Need UX research + broader compatibility tests).
- Interplay with TLS record coalescing and QUIC: would QUIC eliminate many of these issues? Quick experiment planned to try quic-go proxy path.
- Wider scale tests on Dedicated clusters to validate that runtime admission changes don't regress throughput at 10k concurrent streams.

Appendix: quick notes on commands & artifacts used in the run:
- harness: github.com/redwood-inference/stream-probe commit d4f3a2e
- envoy config: test/envoy/progressive-flush/ (filter chain variations)
- measurement script: tools/latency-aggregator/v2/collect.sh --out=run-2026-11-10

- [ ] Build perf regression test for Envoy coalescer filter
- [ ] Schedule canary for runtime arrival-window batching

Notes to self: this doc captures a lot of heuristics — it's worth turning the "what to tune" list into a short public-facing checklist for customers building chatty streaming clients.
